    How this works
    

      
Each flip is one bit from crypto.getRandomValues, the browser's cryptographic source:
        heads when it is 1, tails when it is 0, exactly even odds and no memory of the flip before. A
        thousand flips are a thousand separate bits, not one number spread out. That is a fairer coin than
        the one in your pocket. Real coins lean slightly towards landing the way they started — a 2023 study
        of over 350,000 hand-tossed flips found about 50.8% came down on the starting face — so a person
        who knows which side is up has a small edge. Here there is no starting face.

      
Streaks surprise people, and they should not. In a hundred fair flips the longest run of one face
        is usually six or seven, and a run of eight or more happens in roughly a third of all hundred-flip
        sessions. The page prints the longest run and works out, exactly, how often a fair coin produces a
        run that long in a session that size, so you can see how ordinary it is. It also does not
        balance itself: after five heads, the next flip is still exactly fifty-fifty, and a tally that drifts
        away from half-and-half over a short session is chance, not a fault.

      
The tally since reset lives in this tab only and is gone when it closes. Nothing is sent.

      
The Dark and language buttons remember their settings in this browser's local storage. Nothing you type or drop into the page is stored.
